2 Preliminaries
[id=S2.p1.1] In learning from preferences, we consider a prompt/state space 𝒳\mathcal{X} and a response/action space 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}, the learning algorithm receives as input a starting model πref:𝒳→Δ𝒜\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\Delta_{{\mathcal{A}}} which is usually a model that exits a Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) routine, and a preference dataset of the form 𝒟={Xn,An+,An−}n=1N\mathcal{D}=\left\{{X_{n},A^{+}_{n},A^{-}_{n}}\right\}^{N}_{n=1} where Xn∈𝒳,An+,An−∈𝒜×𝒜X_{n}\in\mathcal{X},A^{+}_{n},A^{-}_{n}\in{\mathcal{A}}\times{\mathcal{A}} for all n∈[N]n\in[N]. In the dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D}, we observe the initial prompts sampled from an initial distribution ν0\nu_{0}, i.e. Xn∼ν0X_{n}\sim\nu_{0} for each n∈[N]n\in[N]. Intuitively, ν0​(x)\nu_{0}(x) is the probability with which a human presents prompt xx to the language model.
Moreover, for each XnX_{n}, 𝒟\mathcal{D} contains two responses An+,An−A^{+}_{n},A^{-}_{n} sampled from an unknown distribution πdata\pi_{\mathrm{data}}.
Moreover, the action An+A^{+}_{n} has been judged the winner over An−A^{-}_{n} by a Bradley-Terry preference model defined as follows.
Definition 2.1.
[id=S2.Thmtheorem1.p1.1] Bradley-Terry (BT) preference model
Given a prompt x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, two responses a,b∈𝒜×𝒜a,b\in{\mathcal{A}}\times{\mathcal{A}} and access to the ground truth reward function r⋆:𝒳×𝒜→[0,Rmax]r^{\star}:\mathcal{X}\times{\mathcal{A}}\rightarrow[0,R_{\max}] for some Rmax∈ℝR_{\max}\in\mathbb{R}, the Bradley-Terry preference model computes the probability of aa being a winner over bb in response to the prompt xx (event denoted as a≻b|xa\succ b|x ) as ℙr⋆true​(a≻b|x)=σ⁡(Δr⋆​(x,a,b))\mathbb{P}^{\mathrm{true}}_{r^{\star}}(a\succ b|x)=\sigma(\Delta_{r^{\star}}(x,a,b))
where Δ𝔣​(x,a,b)=𝔣⁡(x,a)−𝔣⁡(x,b)\Delta_{\mathfrak{f}}(x,a,b)=\mathfrak{f}(x,a)-\mathfrak{f}(x,b) for any function 𝔣:𝒳×𝒜→ℝ\mathfrak{f}:\mathcal{X}\times{\mathcal{A}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} and σ⁡(x)=11+e−x\sigma(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}} denotes the sigmoid function.
[id=S2.Thmtheorem1.p2.1] Given the BT model above, the dataset is labeled sampling Z∼Bernoulli⁡(ℙr⋆true​(a≻b|x))Z\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\mathbb{P}^{\mathrm{true}}_{r^{\star}}(a\succ b|x)) for each x,a,bx,a,b appearing in the dataset. If Z=1Z=1, aa is declared as the winner; vice versa if Z=0Z=0, bb wins the comparison.
[id=S2.p2.1] The goal of the learning algorithm is to update the starting model πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} to obtain a post-trained model πout\pi_{\mathrm{out}} such that it approximately equals
[id=S2.E1]
arg maxπ∈Π⁡Jβ​(π):=⟨π,r⋆⟩−β​K​L​(π,πref)\mathop{\mbox{ arg\,max}}_{\pi\in\Pi}J_{\beta}(\pi):=\left\langle{\pi},{r^{\star}}\right\rangle-\beta KL(\pi,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}})
(1)
[id=S2.p2.2] where Π\Pi is the set of all mappings from prompts to distributions over responses Π={π:𝒳→Δ𝒜}\Pi=\left\{{\pi:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\Delta_{{\mathcal{A}}}}\right\}. The inner product notation is defined for each policy π∈Π\pi\in\Pi and for any function r:𝒳×𝒜→[0,Rmax]r:\mathcal{X}\times{\mathcal{A}}\rightarrow[0,R_{\max}] as ⟨π,r⟩:=∑x,a∈𝒳×𝒜ν0​(x)​π​(a|x)​r​(x,a)\left\langle{\pi},{r}\right\rangle:=\sum_{x,a\in\mathcal{X}\times{\mathcal{A}}}\nu_{0}(x)\pi(a|x)r(x,a) and the average (over prompts) KL is defined for any policy pair π,π′∈Π×Π\pi,\pi^{\prime}\in\Pi\times\Pi as K​L​(π,π′)=∑x,a∈𝒳×𝒜ν0​(x)​π​(a|x)​log⁡π⁡(a|x)/π′​(a|x)KL(\pi,\pi^{\prime})=\sum_{x,a\in\mathcal{X}\times{\mathcal{A}}}\nu_{0}(x)\pi(a|x)\log\nicefrac{{\pi(a|x)}}{{\pi^{\prime}(a|x)}}.
[id=S2.p3.1] The objective in (1) therefore prescribes to find a trade-off between two desiderata: (i) maximizing the ground truth reward r⋆r^{\star} used by the Bradley-Terry preference model to label the dataset and (ii) minimizing the shift as measured by the KL divergence from the initial model πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}. The value of β∈(0,∞)\beta\in(0,\infty) must be set as high as much it is important to stay close to πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} to make sure that πout\pi_{\mathrm{out}} inherits the useful properties learned by πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} from the data observed before entering the learning from preferences phase.
[id=S2.p4.1] We now describe two fundamental ways to solve (1), which will serve as building blocks for our approach.
[id=S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1]
Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: RLHF
[id=S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] In RLHF, the idea is to optimize (1) under two approximations. First, we approximate r⋆r^{\star}, which is unknown to the learner, with the maximum likelihood estimator, denoted by r^\hat{r} and learned on the dataset 𝒟\mathcal{D} as follows:
[id=S2.E2]
r^= arg maxr:𝒳×𝒜→[0,Rmax]∑n=1Nlogσ(Δr(Xn,An+,An−)).\hat{r}=\mathop{\mbox{ arg\,max}}_{r:\mathcal{X}\times{\mathcal{A}}\rightarrow[0,R_{\max}]}\sum^{N}_{n=1}\log\sigma(\Delta_{r}(X_{n},A^{+}_{n},A^{-}_{n})).
(2)
[id=S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.2] Secondly, in (1), the prompt distribution ν0\nu_{0} is unknown; therefore, it must be approximated using, for example, the states observed in the dataset. All in all, RLHF methods output the policy maximizing the following empirical objective over π∈Π\pi\in\Pi,
[id=S2.E3]
∑n=1N∑a∈𝒜π⁡(a|Xn)​(r^​(Xn,a)−β​log⁡π⁡(a|Xn)πref​(a|Xn)).\sum^{N}_{n=1}\sum_{a\in{\mathcal{A}}}\pi(a|X_{n})\left({\hat{r}(X_{n},a)-\beta\log\frac{\pi(a|X_{n})}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(a|X_{n})}}\right).
(3)
[id=S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.3] RLHF has the merit of being the conceptual core of the large majority of, if not all, alignment algorithms. Sadly, it has the drawback of being split into two training steps represented by equations (2) and (3) respectively. This has been elegantly avoided by DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023) with a reparameterization trick explained next.
[id=S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2]
Direct Preference Optimization
[id=S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1] The core observation is that (1), for any reward function rr, admits the following closed form solution
[id=S2.Ex1]
πr​(a|x)=πref​(a|x)​exp⁡(r⁡(x,a)β)Zr​(x),\pi_{r}(a|x)=\frac{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(a|x)\exp(\frac{r(x,a)}{\beta})}{Z_{r}(x)},

Albeit, being incomputable due to the hardness of computing Zr​(x)Z_{r}(x) (unless the reward takes a very specific form (Matrenok et al., 2025)), the closed form expression for πr\pi_{r} allows to write the reward function as
[id=S2.Ex2]
r⁡(x,a)=β​log⁡πr​(a|x)/πref​(a|x)+β​log⁡Zr​(x).r(x,a)=\beta\log\nicefrac{{\pi_{r}(a|x)}}{{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(a|x)}}+\beta\log Z_{r}(x).

(4)
[id=S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.4] Importantly, we have used that for each reward rr, β​Δlog⁡πr/πref​(x,a,b):=β​log⁡πr​(a|x)πref​(a|x)−β​log⁡πr​(b|x)πref​(b|x)\beta\Delta_{\log\pi_{r}/\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}}(x,a,b):=\beta\log\frac{\pi_{r}(a|x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(a|x)}-\beta\log\frac{\pi_{r}(b|x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(b|x)} equals Δr​(x,a,b)\Delta_{r}(x,a,b) because the normalization constant Z⁡(x)Z(x) cancels out.
[id=S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3]
Limitations of RLHF and DPO (i.e., the lack of pessimism):
[id=S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1] The missing ingredient above is that both method maximizes r^\hat{r} (directly or indirectly) blindly, i.e., treating it as if it were a perfect estimate of the ground truth r⋆r^{\star}. However, in practical situations where NN is finite, this is not the case: r^\hat{r} might not be accurate, and taking into account its uncertainty becomes fundamentally important. As an example, think of a single state, two actions case in which r^​(a1)=r^​(a2)+ϵ\hat{r}(a_{1})=\hat{r}(a_{2})+\epsilon for some small ϵ\epsilon but the uncertainty55
5
We keep uncertainty vague here for the sake of intuition. of r^​(a1)\hat{r}(a_{1}) is much higher than r^​(a2)\hat{r}(a_{2}). Then, choosing a2a_{2} is more reasonable while RHLF and DPO, which purely maximize r^\hat{r} would output the highly risky action a1a_{1}.
In a less toy example targeted to LLMs, DPO and RLHF might achieve high reward under r^\hat{r} exploiting hallucinations of r^\hat{r}, i.e., actions that have in fact small reward under the ground truth r⋆r^{\star}.
[id=S2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1] To mitigate these issues, the next section presents our techniques to incorporate pessimism in DPO. In contrast to previous pessimistic DPO versions (Huang et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024b), we assume no knowledge at all of πdata\pi_{\mathrm{data}} whereas (Huang et al., 2024) assumed that πdata=πref\pi_{\mathrm{data}}=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} and (Liu et al., 2024b) leverages access to a policy πbase\pi_{\mathrm{base}} such that ‖πbase/πdata‖∞\left\|{\nicefrac{{\pi_{\mathrm{base}}}}{{\pi_{\mathrm{data}}}}}\right\|_{\infty} is small.

4 Theoretical Guarantees
[id=S4.p1.1] We present here the theoretical guarantees for PEPO, focusing on the tabular setting where the number of prompts and responses are finite.
Our theoretical goal is to quantify the required dataset size NN, so that with high probability Jβ​(π⋆)−Jβ​(πout)≤εJ_{\beta}(\pi^{\star})-J_{\beta}(\pi_{\mathrm{out}})\leq\varepsilon for any policy π⋆∈Π\pi^{\star}\in\Pi. In words, we want the suboptimality of the policy learned by PEPO w.r.t. the comparator π⋆\pi^{\star} to be at most ε\varepsilon.
In particular, as motivated by (Huang et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024b) the gold standard for arguing that over-optimization is avoided is to prove a bound on NN scaling only with a single-policy concentrability coefficient defined as
[id=S4.Ex11]
C⋆:=∑x∈𝒳ν0​(x)​∑a∈𝒜(π⋆​(a|x))2πdata​(a|x).C^{\star}:=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\nu_{0}(x)\sum_{a\in{\mathcal{A}}}\frac{(\pi^{\star}(a|x))^{2}}{\pi_{\mathrm{data}}(a|x)}.
[id=S4.p1.2] In stark contrast, methods prone to overoptimization such as DPO incur an all-policy concentrability coefficient (Song et al., 2024) defined as
Call:=max⁡∑x∈𝒳π∈Π⁡ν0​(x)​∑a∈𝒜(π⁡(a|x))2πdata​(a|x).C^{\mathrm{all}}:=\max_{\pi\in\Pi}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\nu_{0}(x)\sum_{a\in{\mathcal{A}}}\frac{(\pi(a|x))^{2}}{\pi_{\mathrm{data}}(a|x)}.
We highlight that C⋆C^{\star} and CallC^{\mathrm{all}} have strongly different qualitative behaviors. On the one hand, C⋆C^{\star} is reasonably small as soon as sampling from πdata\pi_{\mathrm{data}} allows to observe with high enough probability all the actions which are often chosen by π⋆\pi^{\star}. On the other hand, CallC^{\mathrm{all}} imposes basically to observe with positive probability all possible responses in the dataset 88

[id=S5]
5 Experiments
[id=S5.p1.1] In this section, we show that PEPO successfully avoids over-optimization in LLMs post-training, and we set up a toy experiment to compare the different behaviors of PEPO and χ2\chi^{2}PO in the πref≠πdata\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\neq\pi_{\mathrm{data}} or πref=πdata\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}=\pi_{\mathrm{data}} regimes. Moreover, we notice that rejection sampling can lead to slower generation time. To address this issue, we implement a token-level version of PEPO, which is only an approximation of our theoretically motivated algorithm, but it is faster at generation time while still not showing signs of over-optimization.
[id=S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1]
Rejection Sampling vs Token Level PEPO
[id=S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1] We consider the ensemble of policies generated by finetuning the base model Llama-3.1-8B by running independent instances of DPO for the number of epochs reported in Table 1, and we compare two different pessimistic aggregation rules: the rejection sampling routine in Algorithm 2 and the token-level implementation of PEPO described in Section A.4. The results in Table 1 show that rejection sampling leads to better performances, but token-level PEPO is faster at generation time. Thus, we use the latter for our large-scale experiments presented next.

[id=S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2]
PEPO avoids over-optimization
[id=S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1] Our experiments in Figure 1 clearly show that DPO over-optimizes: the win rate increases during the first few epochs but then drops off significantly. This effect is evident for all base models we experimented with. In contrast, PEPO consistently maintains higher win rates throughout training. These results show that avoiding the CallC^{\mathrm{all}} dependence in the theoretical analysis translates into avoiding over-optimization in practice.
[id=S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3]
Comparison to χ2\chi^{2}PO and SFT+DPO
[id=S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1] We compare PEPO against two methods specifically designed to mitigate over-optimization: χ2\chi^{2}PO and SFT+DPO. As shown in Table 2, PEPO consistently outperforms both baselines across the models we evaluate.

[id=S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1] Crucially, our experimental setup uses the UltraFeedback dataset, where the responses are generated by a diverse pool of LLMs (including proprietary models like GPT-4), meaning that πdata≠πref\pi_{\mathrm{data}}\neq\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}. This distributional mismatch is precisely the setting where χ2\chi^{2}PO and SFT+DPO lose their theoretical guarantees, as both methods rely on exact or approximate knowledge of πdata\pi_{\mathrm{data}}. PEPO, by contrast, achieves pessimism through ensemble agreement rather than regularization toward a known reference distribution, allowing it to succeed even when πdata\pi_{\mathrm{data}} is unknown. We hypothesize that the performance gap would likely narrow in an experimental setting where the preference dataset is generated directly from πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} (i.e., πdata=πref\pi_{\mathrm{data}}=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}), as this would restore the conditions under which χ2\chi^{2}PO and SFT+DPO are theoretically sound.

[id=A1.SS4]
A.4 On the token level implementation of PEPO
[id=A1.SS4.p1.1] As mentioned in the main text, we also introduce a version for PEPO which implements the pessimistic aggregation rule given by Lemma 3.2 at the token level rather than the trajectory level. This approach is faster at generation time because it does not reject generations, while Algorithm 2 does. In practice, this translates to a 3x speed at generation time, therefore we preferred this version for most of our large-scale evaluations.
[id=A1.SS4.p2.1] While our theoretical guarantees do not hold for the token level version of PEPO we can notice that the token level aggregation rule is even more pessimistic than the trajectory level version. Indeed, notice that our notion of worst case implicit reward over the ensemble can be lower bounded by a token level worst case reward as follows. [id=A1.SS5]
A.5 Details for the large scale experiments
[id=A1.SS5.p1.1] This section describes how to implement PEPO efficiently in practice.
[id=A1.SS5.SSS1]
A.5.1 Models and Fine-Tuning Setup
[id=A1.SS5.SSS1.p1.1] We evaluate PEPO on four instruction-tuned language models spanning a range of sizes. At the 7–8B scale, we consider Llama-3.1-Tulu-3-8B-SFT, which serves as a strong open-source baseline, along with Zephyr-7B-SFT and Mistral-7B-SFT. To demonstrate scalability, we also include Yi-34B-Chat, a 34B parameter model. All backbone models have undergone supervised fine-tuning (SFT) prior to preference optimization.
[id=A1.SS5.SSS1.p2.1] Rather than full fine-tuning, we employ Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [Hu et al., 2022] for parameter-efficient training. All LoRA adapters use rank r=16r=16 with scaling factor α=16\alpha=16 (the low-rank updates are scaled by α/r\alpha/r), a dropout rate of 5%, and are applied to all linear layers in the model. This adds approximately 0.5-1.5% (depending on the model) parameters which are trainable while the backbone stays frozen.
[id=A1.SS5.SSS1.Px1]
Memory Efficiency of the Ensemble.
[id=A1.SS5.SSS1.Px1.p1.1] A crucial practical advantage of PEPO is that maintaining an ensemble of LL models does not require LL times more GPU memory compared to a single model. Since all ensemble members share the same frozen backbone and only differ in their lightweight LoRA adapters, the total memory footprint is approximately Mbase+L⋅MadapterM_{\text{base}}+L\cdot M_{\text{adapter}} rather than L⋅MbaseL\cdot M_{\text{base}}. Given that each adapter constitutes only small fraction of the base model size, the memory overhead of the ensemble is modest even for moderate values of LL. The schematic implementation of this process is shown in .

[id=A1.SS5.SSS2]
A.5.2 Dataset and Preprocessing
[id=A1.SS5.SSS2.p1.1] For all large-scale experiments, we utilize the UltraFeedback Binarized dataset [Cui et al., 2023]. This version is derived from the original UltraFeedback corpus by "binarizing" multi-model outputs into discrete preference pairs. Specifically, for each prompt, four responses were generated by diverse language models and scored by GPT-4 across multiple dimensions (e.g., helpfulness and honesty). The binarized version identifies the highest-scoring response as the chosen sample and selects one of the remaining lower-scoring responses as the rejected sample. We use the standard train_sft split for training and test_sft for validation. However, we note that the validation loss is a poor proxy for downstream evaluation performance (e.g., AlpacaEval win rate), making early stopping based on this metric unreliable. This further underscores the need for methods like PEPO that are inherently robust to overoptimization.
[id=A1.SS5.SSS2.p2.1] During preprocessing, we truncate sequences to a maximum length of 1024 tokens, with prompts limited to 512 tokens to ensure sufficient space for generated responses.
[id=A1.SS5.SSS2.Px1]
Data Partitioning.
[id=A1.SS5.SSS2.Px1.p1.1] For PEPO, we partition the training data into LL disjoint subsets of approximately equal size, where LL is the ensemble size. This partitioning ensures statistical independence across ensemble members, as required by our theoretical analysis (Lemma 4.2). We note that in practice, data efficiency could potentially be improved by using overlapping subsets, though we leave this exploration to future work.
[id=A1.SS5.SSS3]
A.5.3 Training Procedure
[id=A1.SS5.SSS3.p1.1] We train all models using the AdamW optimizer with bfloat16 mixed precision for computational efficiency. Training is carried out with a learning rate of 1×10−51\times 10^{-5} and a weight decay of 0.010.01. We maintain a consistent effective batch size of 64 across all experiments, using gradient accumulation where necessary. To accelerate training, we pre-compute and cache the reference model’s log-probabilities for all training examples, avoiding redundant forward passes through the frozen backbone.
[id=A1.SS5.SSS3.p2.1] For PEPO, the β\beta parameter controlling KL regularization is set to 0.1, matching the DPO baseline. We set the pessimism parameter B​𝔭tie¯B\overline{\mathfrak{p}_{\mathrm{tie}}} (denoted as α\alpha in our codebase) to 0.1. While our theory suggests this term should be state-dependent, we treat it as a constant prompt-response independent hyperparameter in practice for simplicity. We conducted a preliminary ablation on the value of this parameter, but observed no substantial difference in downstream performance within this range. We ablate the ensemble size L∈{2,3,4}L\in\{2,3,4\} to understand the trade-off between pessimism strength and data efficiency. Note that L=1L=1 corresponds to a single model trained with the pessimistic DPO loss, while L=1L=1 with the pessimism parameter α\alpha set to 0 recovers the standard DPO.
[id=A1.SS5.SSS3.p3.1] For the baselines, χ2\chi^{2}PO uses β=0.1\beta=0.1, γ=1.0\gamma=1.0, and Rmax=10.0R_{\max}=10.0 with internal gradient clipping, following the original paper. SFT+DPO combines the DPO objective with a supervised fine-tuning regularizer weighted by λSFT=0.005\lambda_{\text{SFT}}=0.005. In SFT+DPO we use chosen as well as rejected answers from the UltraFeedback as an estimate for πdata\pi_{\mathrm{data}}. All experiments use seed 42 for reproducibility.
[id=A1.SS5.SSS4]
A.5.4 Ensemble Training and Inference
[id=A1.SS5.SSS4.p1.1] The PEPO ensemble is trained by assigning each LoRA adapter to its corresponding data partition. Ensemble members can be trained sequentially or in parallel across multiple GPUs without any required communication between the members of the ensemble. Therefore, the training of all LL LoRA adapters can be carried out in parallel as shown in .
[id=A1.SS5.SSS4.p2.1] While we introduced a rejection sampling scheme in Section 3 that samples exactly from πout\pi_{\mathrm{out}}, it can be computationally expensive at inference time. For our large-scale experiments, we instead employ the token-level approximation detailed in Section A.4. This variant applies the pessimistic aggregation at each decoding step, enabling efficient autoregressive generation. We use greedy decoding (temperature T=0T=0) with this token-level aggregation for all reported unless stated otherwise.
[id=A1.SS5.SSS4.Px1]
Shared backbone inference
[id=A1.SS5.SSS4.Px1.p1.1] During inference of PEPO, we load multiple adapters together with one shared backbone. This allows us to efficiently switch the adapters on and off to run the forward pass with different members of the ensemble without reloading the model to and from device each time. We make use of multiple GPUS by distributing multiple copies of this shared backbone model on each available device. This is shown in .
[id=A1.SS5.SSS5]
A.5.5 Evaluation Protocol
[id=A1.SS5.SSS5.p1.1] We evaluate all models on AlpacaEval [Li et al., 2023a], a benchmark that measures pairwise win rate against a reference model across 805 diverse prompts spanning open-ended generation, reasoning, and instruction-following tasks. We report the win rate against the initial (epoch 0) SFT model, which measures the improvement from preference optimization. To ensure reproducibility and manage costs, we use Llama-3-70B-Instruct as the preference judge (run locally), utilizing the alpaca_eval_llama3_70b_fn configuration.
[id=A1.SS5.SSS5.p2.1] All responses are generated using a maximum of 1024 new tokens. We evaluate model checkpoints at every training epoch to capture learning dynamics and potential over-optimization. The win rates reported in the Table 2 correspond to the epoch checkpoint generated by each algorithm.
[id=A1.SS5.SSS6]
A.5.6 Computational Resources
[id=A1.SS5.SSS6.p1.1] Experiments were conducted on NVIDIA GH200 120GB and NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB GPUs. We allocated one GPU per ensemble member for training (e.g., 4 GPUs for a PEPO model with L=4L=4, trained in parallel) and two GPUs for evaluation and generation (mainly to accommodate the Llama-3-70B-Instruct judge). Since we parallelize the training of the ensemble across devices and partition the dataset such that each member sees only 1/L1/L of the data, the wall-clock time required for training is significantly reduced (roughly proportional to 1/L1/L) compared to training a single model on the full dataset.
[id=A1.SS5.SSS6.p2.1] For training, we observed that the average wall-clock time per epoch for the Llama-3-8B model dropped from 3.61 hours (L=1L=1) to 0.90 hours (L=4L=4). Similarly, for Yi-34B, training took approximately 4.0 hours per epoch with L=4L=4.
[id=A1.SS5.SSS6.p3.1] For evaluation on AlpacaEval, generating responses and computing win rates using the token-level sampling detailed in Section A.4 for the 8B model takes approximately 30 minutes on a single NVIDIA GH200 GPU and approximately 1.25 hours on an NVIDIA A100 GPU. In contrast, full rejection sampling using the minimum probability criterion is prohibitively expensive. While this method remains efficient in early training updates—achieving a strong 67.77% win rate on Llama-3-8B, we observe that the acceptance probability quickly collapses (α→0\alpha\to 0) as the ensemble diverges. This causes the generator to saturate the trial limit (∼16\sim 16 attempts per answer), increasing the evaluation time to approximately 80 hours on an NVIDIA A100 GPU. However, an optimized variant using mean and standard deviation criteria mitigates this collapse, maintaining a high acceptance rate (α≈0.8\alpha\approx 0.8) and low overhead (∼1.2\sim 1.2 attempts per answer). While this optimized variant reduces the runtime to around 4 hours, it remains significantly slower (8×8\times) than the greedy approach. This vast difference in computational cost—without a corresponding gain in performance—justifies our choice of the efficient token-level approximation for large-scale benchmarks.
